articles.title_orig: Across southwest China and Thailand, plant turnover and nematode body width help explain soil diversity
articles.title_zh: Across southwest China and Thailand, plant turnover and nematode body width help explain soil diversity
articles.content_orig:
Across southwest China and Thailand, plant turnover and nematode body width help explain soil diversity
Soils harbor some of the most diverse life on Earth. Soil nematodes play crucial roles in maintaining ecosystem functions. Yet how their diversity changes across large landscapes, and what drives those changes, remains poorly understood.
In a new study published in PNAS on Sept. 22, researchers from the Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden (XTBG) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and their collaborators found that plant community turnover and nematode body width play fundamental roles in shaping soil nematode diversity across different spatial scales. Their findings highlight that protecting the variety of plant species is essential for preserving nematode diversity and that a nematode's body width largely determines how it spreads through the environment.
Forests sampled across a mountain transect
The researchers conducted their study across southwest China and Thailand. Using a nested sampling design, they collected about 700 soil samples from seven undisturbed forest plots, each measuring 400 × 400 meters (1,310 × 1,310 feet). The plots included two coniferous forests, two broadleaf forests and three tropical rainforests, with 40 × 40-meter (130 × 130-foot) grids serving as the smallest sampling units.
"By examining nematode communities along a montane forest transect spanning the Tibetan Plateau, Hengduan Mountains, and tropical lowlands, we were able to uncover how the drivers of soil nematode diversity change across spatial scales," said Wang Wenting, first author of the study.
Plant turnover tracks underground diversity
They identified 209 nematode genera across five feeding types (including herbivores, bacterivores, fungivores, omnivores and predators). Tropical rainforests supported the highest nematode diversity among the forest types examined.
Nematode α-diversity and γ-diversity consistently increased with plant β-diversity across most feeding types. This underscores that maintaining a mosaic of different plant communities is critical for safeguarding biodiversity underground.
Body width shapes dispersal
The researchers also found that a nematode's body width, rather than its length, is a key trait influencing how its community assembles. Body length had little effect on assembly processes, except for random changes known as "ecological drift." This suggests that body width may play a more important role in limiting how far nematodes can disperse.
"Our findings demonstrate that aboveground and belowground biodiversity are tightly linked with the turnover in plant species from one location to another. Protecting ecosystems and biodiversity is not just about conserving plants; it's about safeguarding the invisible majority of life beneath our feet," said Yang Xiaodong of XTBG.

articles.title_orig: Trump rolls out the red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping despite U.S.-China tensions
articles.title_zh: Trump rolls out the red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping despite U.S.-China tensions
articles.content_orig:
Trump rolls out the red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping despite U.S.-China tensions
Washington — President Trump is offering a warm welcome to Chinese President Xi Jinping this week as the U.S. tries to choke China's supply of semiconductor chips for artificial intelligence advancement, as the two countries determine whether their fragile truce on tariffs will continue, and as concerns mount about China's relationships with Iran and Russia.
Xi's visit to the White House, the first in more than a decade, features a state arrival ceremony Wednesday, with Mr. Trump taking part along with U.S. military personnel.
Thursday will bring a formal meeting of the two presidents and a state dinner. Xi's wife, Peng Liyuan, is joining the trip.
Mr. Trump and Xi last met in May, when Xi welcomed the U.S. president for a state visit in Beijing.
What to expect on the schedule
Mr. Trump welcomed Xi and his wife at Joint Base Andrews late Wednesday, a rare instance of a sitting president greeting a foreign leader on the tarmac instead of awaiting them at the White House.
A military band played as Xi and his wife exited a massive Air China jet while the American president and first lady awaited them on a red carpet at the bottom of the stairs. The arrival ceremony, which included a flyover with two B-1 bombers, was quick, and Mr. Trump and the first lady departed about 10 minutes later.
Later Wednesday, the Chinese government provided an arrival statement on behalf of Xi. "China and the United States should be partners, not rivals," the statement reads. Xi says he seeks bilateral ties where "cooperation is the mainstay, competition is kept within proper limits, differences are managed and peace can be expected."
On Thursday morning, the president and first lady Melania Trump will host another arrival ceremony for Xi and his wife on the White House South Lawn. The White House says the ceremony will feature nearly 500 service members from all branches of the U.S. military.
The U.S. and Chinese flags will be displayed on the South Portico, according to the White House. The U.S. Marine Band will play the anthems of both the U.S. and China, the White House says. Then, both Mr. Trump and Xi are expected to speak.
The arrival ceremony is also expected to have a military flyover with a B-2 Spirit bomber and four F-22s.
The presidents' spouses are expected to visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art on Thursday while Mr. Trump and Xi meet. A state dinner will be Thursday evening.
On Friday, the couples will have tea at the White House before heading to the National Archives. The visit will then conclude.
China experts say not to expect many big policy achievements
China experts say to not expect many tangible policy outcomes from the meeting. James Lewis, a distinguished fellow with the Tech Policy Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, said there "isn't much of a formal agenda" for the two leaders.
"I'm not anticipating very much — I don't think anyone is," Lewis said. "Because this is largely for show. And it's largely a discussion between two very cautious and two very suspicious leaders."
"I don't think there's too much hope for policy achievements," said Jake Werner, director of the East Asia Program at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.
"Probably more than anything, Trump loves a show," Werner added. "He loves to put on a show. And secondarily, he thinks he has a relationship with Xi Jinping, who he thinks is a big, strong man, and he values those sorts of relationships. And then I think … he has a desire to make sure that China doesn't use the power that it demonstrated that it has last year when it cut the U.S. off of rare-earth elements, and American factories started shutting down."
Mr. Trump has often praised Xi and cast his warm personal relationship with the Chinese leader as an asset. During his visit to Beijing earlier this year, Mr. Trump called Xi a "great leader" and said the two men have always been able to work out their disagreements.
As for the disagreements that could dominate this week's visit: This is the meeting of the three "Ts," as Lewis put it — trade, tech and Taiwan.
What Trump and Xi may discuss on tariffs and trade
On trade, the U.S. and China will have to decide whether to extend a truce on tariffs that expires on Nov. 10.
That deal, struck in Busan, South Korea, in October, lowered tariffs levied by both countries and paused restrictions on Chinese exports of rare earth minerals. It also said China would continue to buy large quantities of U.S. soybeans, a pledge China has failed to keep.
The truce allowed the two countries to climb down from a tit-for-tat trade war that sent U.S. and Chinese tariffs to more than 100% at one point in spring 2025.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng over the weekend, said the Chinese have proposed a "bigger deal" on trade between the U.S. and China, beyond the trade truce brokered in Busan, South Korea, in October.
Bessent said Mr. Trump and Xi may meet "up to four times" this year, so they're open to different approaches. Thursday will be their second meeting.
"We're open to the idea of just continuing the Busan arrangement, or examining the bigger deal," Bessent told reporters Wednesday. "We're fine with both, and we're going to do what's best for the American people."
On Fox News Monday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said there will be an announcement establishing a U.S.-China "Board of Trade," which will determine a "relatively small subset of goods" that the two countries agree they should protect from trade disputes. That may include things like low-tech consumer goods and some agricultural products, Greer said. The idea of such a board was discussed when Mr. Trump and Xi met in May.
Trump and Xi may discuss artificial intelligence
Amid growing public pressure for the U.S. government to implement more safeguards around advanced artificial intelligence, Bessent shared over the weekend that the U.S. has proposed a new "notification system" alerting AI incidents that affect national security. He made the announcement following a meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.
"We want a shared vision of common goals and common threats," Bessent said, according to the Associated Press. "We think that just like any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the No. 1 and the No. 2 AI powers in the world is very important."
It's not yet clear if Mr. Trump is on board with that idea. His most-voiced concern about AI is the need for the U.S. to beat China, and he has spoken out against the idea of reining in the speed of AI research. He slowed and altered an executive order allowing the government to voluntarily review the latest frontier AI models before they are released.
Lewis said Xi wants access to advanced computer chips and to be able to sell memory chips to the U.S. Nvidia, one of the leading designers of the chips that power AI models, is currently prohibited from selling its most advanced products in China, though Mr. Trump has allowed it to sell its H200 chips to "approved customers."
There is also growing concern that Chinese AI developers are using a method called "distillation" to train Chinese AI models based on U.S. frontier models, according to the federal government's Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
AI is on the Trump-Xi agenda, a White House official told reporters on a call Friday on the condition of anonymity, although the person didn't elaborate. A reporter asked the White House official if the president will have a substantive call with Xi about AI safety, and if Mr. Trump is prepared to extend or renew the existing semiconductor chip-related licenses with China.
"Those are both on the agenda, both AI and the current 'Busan' truce, and we'll know more once the two leaders meet," the White House official said.

articles.title_zh: Opinion | China’s top priority should be wages, not AI
articles.content_orig:
China’s top priority should be wages, not AI
China’s pressing economic problem is that ordinary people still have too little money in their pockets
Lijia Zhang is a rocket-factory worker turned social commentator, and the author of a novel, Lotus.
“Whoever wins with AI wins,” US President Donald Trump has declared, dismissing warnings about the risks of developing artificial intelligence too rapidly and citing rivalry with China.
The technological competition is real. China has reason to fear becoming dependent on America for advanced chips and AI technology, particularly as Washington has repeatedly restricted its access to cutting-edge semiconductors. China, meanwhile, is directing enormous resources towards AI. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index estimates that Chinese government guidance funds deployed US$184 billion into AI-related companies between 2000 and 2023.
I am no technology expert. But as someone who spent 10 years greasing machine parts in a factory, I wonder whether China has got its priorities right. Should winning the AI race be such an overriding national ambition when the country has another pressing economic problem? Namely, ordinary Chinese people still have too little money in their pockets.

articles.title_orig: McDonald’s to take on KFC and rivals as Gen Z flock to fried chicken
articles.title_zh: McDonald’s to take on KFC and rivals as Gen Z flock to fried chicken
articles.content_orig:
McDonald’s is betting on fried chicken as health concerns and the rising price of beef shift dining habits.
The company said that it aimed to take an extra 1.5 percentage point-share of the global chicken market by 2030, with an aim to increase its share of drinks by the same proportion. McDonald’s said the growth in chicken, a lower-priced protein, would not come at the expense of beef burger sales, saying it aimed maintain its “leadership position in beef”.
Chris Kempczinski, McDonald’s chair and chief executive, told investors in May that the chain’s share of the chicken market was in the “high teens”, compared with about 45% in beef, but the chicken market was bigger and growing at twice the pace of its red meat counterpart.
McDonald’s has warned that the rising cost of beef, as well as energy, was hitting profits for its franchisees. The chain also faces heavy competition from the rapid rise of chicken shop chains including Popeyes and Wingstop as well as expansion by the more established player KFC, driven particularly by the popularity of fried chicken among younger Gen Z consumers.
“McDonald’s has the unmatched scale, customer insights, brand loyalty and operational capabilities to not only adapt to the next wave of change in our industry, but to turn it into an advantage,” said Kempczinski.
The chain also said it would spend about $8.5bn (£6.4bn) to help franchisees with rent and improve their restaurants.
The change comes amid the rapid rise in chicken shops and sales of chicken and the surging price of beef, which has risen by more than 20% in the past two years in the US and the UK, according to figures from the UK’s Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board.
Peter Backman, an independent food service industry analyst, said “chicken is cheaper and perceived as healthier”.
He said the rising price of beef was likely to be a “drag on the market” for burgers and offering more chicken would enable McDonald’s to sell more to its fans and “steal a bit of market share from other quick service operators”. He said higher drinks sales were probably attractive as beverages tended to be more profitable.
In the UK, 39% of consumers used chicken shops in 2025 compared with 37% in 2023, according to market research firm Mintel, with Gen Z usage hitting 52%, almost matching pizza outlets at 56%. A plethora of other options, including Asian-inspired chains such as Wagamama, are also eating into the market share of burgers and pizza.
Late last year Domino’s Pizza Group announced that its chief executive of two years had stepped down with immediate effect, less than two weeks after he appeared to suggest the UK may be approaching “peak pizza” and that the chain should try to broaden its menu to sell more chicken.

articles.title_orig: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction
articles.title_zh: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction
articles.content_orig:
Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years on Wednesday after being convicted of sexually assaulting former TV production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006 at his Manhattan apartment.
Haley appeared in court on Wednesday morning and delivered a victim impact statement.
In her statement, Haley spoke about the harassment and humiliation she has endured over the past seven years, saying she was publicly smeared by Weinstein, his defense team, and podcasters she suspects were paid to damage her image.
Haley added that her experience following the assault has “already been a life sentence” for her, and asked the judge to take all of this into consideration.
New York assistant district attorney Nicole Blumberg addressed the court on behalf of the prosecution. She asked the court to sentence Weinstein, 74, to 20 years with five years of post-release supervision, stating he never showed any type of remorse for his crimes.
Weinstein said in his statement he has remorse for Haley. “I live with many regrets and sincerely apologize for my actions,” he said.
Weinstein’s defense had also argued that their client is too sick to serve a long sentence following a diagnosis of several health conditions including blood cancer and heart disease. The defense asked for a nine-year sentence.
Before sentencing, Judge Curtis Farber acknowledged that Weinstein would be remembered not just for producing films, but for being the face of the #MeToo movement. Farber said Weinstein took advantage of Haley’s dreams of working in the film industry.
“You had it all,” Farber said. “Your legacy could have been cemented with greatness. But you threw it all away by assaulting Miriam Haley.”
The latest sentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in the closely watched case.
Weinstein was sentenced to 23 years in prison in 2020 after a jury convicted him of sexually assaulting Haley and raping aspiring actor Jessica Mann.
But in 2024, New York’s highest court overturned the convictions, saying Weinstein’s trial had been prejudiced by the judge allowing woman who alleged they were sexual assault victims of Weinstein to testify, despite not being plaintiffs in the case.
Weinstein went on trial again in 2025 and was once more convicted of a criminal sexual act involving Haley.
Jurors acquitted Weinstein of a separate sexual assault charge involving former model Kaja Sokola but could not reach a verdict on the rape charge involving Mann. Prosecutors retried the Mann charge earlier this year, but the jury deadlocked in May. The charge was later dropped after Mann said she could not endure another trial.
Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate California rape case.
In June, a California appeals court upheld Weinstein’s 2022 rape and sexual assault conviction. He was found guilty of assaulting an Italian model in her hotel room during a film festival.
He could serve the California sentence before beginning the sentence imposed in New York. Farber said at Wednesday’s sentencing that California will have the final say on whether Weinstein’s sentences run consecutively or concurrently.
The accusations and subsequent charges against Weinstein were one of the biggest factors in launching the #MeToo movement. More than 80 women have come forward with allegations of sexual assault or misconduct against him.

articles.title_zh: Jacoby Brissett: No one has lost confidence in Marvin Harrison Jr.
articles.content_orig:
Marvin Harrison Jr. hasn’t been the wide receiver the Cardinals thought they were getting when they drafted him fourth overall in 2024. That’s something everyone can agree.
The Cardinals, though, are pushing back against the narrative surrounding Harrison’s slow start to 2026.
A viral video, viewed more than 18 million times, started the discussion about Harrison’s effort level. Other videos have since questioned whether Harrison is giving 100 percent.
Quarterback Jacoby Brissett and coach Mike LaFleur defended Harrison on Wednesday.
“When you talk about his work ethic and you talk about him showing up and being engaged in the meetings and then going out on the field and giving 110 percent and being the Marv we all know he is, that hasn’t changed,” Brissett said, via Tyler Drake of Arizona Sports.
“Nobody’s lost confidence in Marv. The hard part as a young player is the noise from the outside telling you what they expect from you and the things of that nature. Does Marv want the ball? Yes. Do we understand that he wants the ball? Yes. Is it only Week 2? Yes. . . . At some point, the tide will change. When? We don’t know yet. Hopefully soon.”
Harrison has seen four targets, with one catch for 33 yards this season.
LaFleur was asked on Monday about Harrison jogging through routes.
“I don’t see it that way. I think his running style is different from some other people’s,” LaFleur said. “If that’s people’s narrative on him, that’s fine, but I know his teammates don’t feel that way.”
LaFleur doubled down Wednesday.
“In between those walls, Marv is Marv,” he said. “He’s attacking it every single day like he always does, just like his teammates do. I appreciate the way he goes about his business.”
As for whether Harrison’s run-blocking needs to improve, LaFleur said everyone’s “efforts need to improve.”
Dan Graziano of ESPN talked to league executives who wondered whether the Cardinals will shop Harrison before the trade deadline. The Texans are among the teams that could be in the market for help at the position.

articles.title_orig: Some climb for faith, others for the views. This Chinese sacred mountain draws them all
articles.title_zh: Some climb for faith, others for the views. This Chinese sacred mountain draws them all
articles.content_orig:
WUDANG, China (AP) — A banknote clasped between her hands, Liu Haiyan prayed to the protector of the Wudang mountains. The range in central China has long been considered sacred in Taoism.
“I asked him to bless our motherland with favorable weather and to make it even more prosperous,” Liu said while sitting outside the Golden Hall, a Taoist temple at the summit of Tianzhu Peak.
“This place watches over our country,” she added. “We’re Chinese and this is part of our faith.”
Tourists and pilgrims in a steady stream make their way through Wudang every day. Its scenic peaks, ancient palaces and religious sites drew 14 million visits in 2025, according to government figures.
Wudang’s Taoist buildings date as far back as the 7th century. The complex expanded over centuries through China’s Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties.
Liu traveled several hundred kilometers (miles) from Hebei province with her daughter, Ji Jiaxin. She also prayed to Wudang’s protector, known as Zhenwu.
“He can guide people toward goodness,” Ji said. “He also watches over all the living things that grow across the land.”
Both women see Wudang as a place of scenic beauty and spiritual significance. Perched at about 1,610 meters (5,280 feet) above sea level, the Golden Hall is a place where they experience a sense of spiritual purification.
“Everyone comes here with a sincere heart,” Liu said. “With sincerity, the divine will respond.”
Philosophy and symbolism are woven into Wudang’s conception
The Wudang mountain range comprises 72 peaks, all thought to converge toward Tianzhu. Its lower slopes are associated with fire, while the deity enshrined at its summit is linked to water.
“Water at the top can moisten the earth, while fire below provides warmth and enables all living things to grow,” said Shu Chenghai, director of social education at Wudang Museum.
The Golden Hall’s construction reflects this symbolism too.
In the traditional Chinese concept of the Five Elements, metal is believed to generate water. And since natural sources can run dry over time, the bronze hall serves as a means to nourish Heaven and Earth.
“It embodies prayers for favorable weather, abundant harvests and peace and prosperity throughout the country,” Shu said.
Generations built their lives around Wudang’s temples
Taoist priests and monks look after the religious sites throughout Wudang. With their hair tied in high buns and dressed in distinctive blue robes, they glide through the temples, talking to visitors and scanning tickets at the entrances.
Their role also connects Wudang’s spiritual life with the communities that call the mountain home.
Cai Hongping was born in the area. Her family settled beside Zixiao Palace, a major Taoist temple complex.
“Some of the elderly Taoist priests there were exceptionally kind and compassionate,” Cai said. “Sometimes they gave us dates, peanuts or fruit.”
Life in the mountains was difficult when Cai was a child. Food and other material goods were scarce, but she remembers the temples as places of happiness and joy.
“I often went with the Taoist priests to identify Chinese medicinal herbs, practiced martial arts with them, and sometimes stole fruit that had been left as offerings,” Cai said.
Her connection to the mountain extended beyond its temples.
Cai’s grandfather was a heritage conservation worker in Wudang, a role focused on preserving and cataloging cultural relics. Her father also made walking sticks for visitors. Cai and other relatives sometimes joined him in gathering medicinal herbs to sell.
“The entire mountain was my childhood,” Cai said. “It has also given me a reverence for life.”
Ming emperors left their mark on Wudang
Wudang’s palaces and temples flourished during the Ming dynasty, when Emperor Zhu Di undertook a major building campaign to align his imperial regime with Taoism.
At its height, the complex included dozens of temples, palaces and monasteries. More than 60 sites survive today.
Wudang’s development coincided with another major project commissioned by Zhu Di: the Forbidden City in Beijing.
“When we say, ‘The Forbidden City was built in the north, and Wudang was developed in the south,’ we mean that these two World Cultural Heritage sites are like twins,” Shu said.
“The two places conveyed a message to the world: one represented Heaven, while the other represented the human realm,” he added.
Wudang’s special connection with Ming dynasty emperors remains visible today.
Along the route taken by tourists and pilgrims are several steles marking ritual proclamations made on behalf of emperors during the first year of each reign.
“An emperor needed to make a ritual proclamation to Zhenwu,” Shu said. “He would declare that he had succeeded to the imperial throne and express his hope for Heaven’s support.”
Visitors still seek meaning in Wudang’s landscape
Long before today’s visitors made their way to Wudang, the mountain drew people seeking solitude and spiritual cultivation.
Shu said its distinctive landscape embodies the traditional Chinese concept of “Dong Tian Fu Di,” or “grotto-heavens and blessed lands” — places traditionally regarded as sacred retreats.
“The idea is that a profound harmony between humanity and nature is not merely something human beings can create,” he added.
Beyond the Golden Hall, visitors encounter other temples and figures associated with different needs, from health and inner balance to martial arts.
Wang Xia recently traveled from Inner Mongolia and visited Taizipo, or Prince Slope, a Taoist temple complex linked to Zhenwu’s legendary early life as a prince.
“The fact that the crown prince once studied here makes it particularly appealing,” Wang said. “I wanted to pray for my child, to wish her academic success and a bright future.”
Her first encounter with Wudang came from books. She read about the Ming dynasty and began to dream about visiting the site herself one day.
“I imagined that coming here would give me the feeling of entering the world of Taoist immortals,” Wang said. “That is what this place feels like: a mountain of immortals.”

articles.title_orig: Iowa Judge Dismisses Trump’s Lawsuit Against The Des Moines Register
articles.title_zh: Iowa Judge Dismisses Trump’s Lawsuit Against The Des Moines Register
articles.content_orig:
An Iowa judge has dismissed President Donald Trump’s lawsuit against pollster J. Ann Selzer, her polling company, the Des Moines Register and Gannett.
In a written ruling on Wednesday, Judge Scott Beattie of Iowa’s Fifth Judicial District threw out the lawsuit by Trump, Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and former Iowa State Senator Brad Zaun.
The suit was dismissed with prejudice, which means Trump cannot file the same claim again. The attorneys who represented the president in the personal action did not immediately respond to CNN’s request for comment about whether they intend to appeal.
The ruling marks a setback in Trump’s broader legal campaign against news outlets, including ongoing lawsuits against the BBC, The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal.
The lawsuit centered on a 2024 poll published days before the presidential election that showed Vice President Kamala Harris with a lead in Iowa that did not pan out in the actual election results. The suit alleged that the poll and the reporting around it aimed to artificially give Democrats an edge in the last week of the campaign.
Trump, Miller-Meeks and Zaun accused the defendants of knowingly publishing false polling information and, even if unintentional, negligently publishing false information.
Regarding the claim that the poll violated the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act, Beattie wrote that the “Iowa Poll and its reporting are fully protected political speech,” noting that plaintiffs’ lawsuit “does not allege the elements that would place that speech within the fraud exception.”
But Beattie noted that even if the First Amendment issues were set aside, the claims still didn’t meet Iowa law’s basic requirements. While Trump, Miller-Meeks, and Zaun tried to use the state’s consumer fraud statute, Beattie wrote that it applies only to consumer transactions.
Regarding the alleged fraudulent misrepresentation, Beattie writes that there was “no representation made to induce any plaintiff to act and no act taken in reliance on the truth of the polls.”
The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, the nonprofit free speech group that took up Selzer’s defense, said in a statement, “We’re pleased that the court recognized what we’ve said all along: This lawsuit was laughable from the beginning and never should have been brought.”
“The First Amendment does not allow anyone in government, least of all the president, to punish people under the banner of ‘fake news.’ That may work for him as a campaign slogan, but it is not a thing in the law,” FIRE chief counsel Bob Corn-Revere said.
The First Amendment victory in Iowa came on the same day that a federal judge in Washington heard arguments in CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s lawsuit over Trump’s White House media ban. The judge in that case said he would rule soon.
Des Moines Register owner Gannett, which renamed itself USA Today Co. last year, also celebrated the victory on Wednesday.
“This decision reaffirms the enduring First Amendment principles that empower journalists and sends a message to those who think they can intimidate the press through legal action,” said Polly Grunfeld Sack, the media company’s chief legal counsel.

articles.title_zh: Trump welcomes China's Xi to Washington with planeside ceremony and extension of trade truce

HONG KONG — President Donald Trump’s strong rapport with Xi Jinping is set to be on display in Washington this week as the Chinese leader makes his first U.S. state visit in more than a decade. But below the surface-level pageantry at the White House, little is likely to be resolved as the world’s two biggest economies continue to spar over trade, Taiwan, AI and more.
Since a trade war shook the global economy last year, U.S.-China relations have been at an effective standstill, experts say, buying both sides time to reinforce their strengths and address their vulnerabilities.
Trump, who usually meets with foreign leaders at the White House, was at the tarmac to greet Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, when they arrived at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, outside Washington on Wednesday.
Trump welcomes Xi at Joint Base Andrews
Trump will be greeting Xi in a weaker position than when they last met four months ago, said Allen Carlson, an associate professor of government at Cornell University, as he faces mounting inflation, falling approval ratings, an unpopular war with Iran and a potentially disastrous midterm election result for his Republican Party.
The main issue for Thursday’s summit — whether to extend a fragile trade truce that Trump and Xi agreed to last fall — was resolved before the two leaders had an official meeting.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in an interview on Fox News Wednesday that the U.S. and China have agreed to extend the bilateral trade truce that was set to expire in November through Jan. 10.
The announcement came after Bessent and China’s vice premier, He Lifeng, held an unscheduled meeting in Washington.
Another key issue is artificial intelligence, which is increasingly at the center of U.S.-China competition. Warnings from American AI leaders that the technology could pose an existential threat have raised fears about the ability of the world’s two leading AI powers to work together to contain its potential dangers.
Bessent said Sunday after preparatory talks with Chinese officials that the U.S. had proposed exchanging safety alerts with China for AI-related incidents that could affect national security. But experts say it’s unlikely that this week’s summit will produce any major security agreement on AI.
That leaves the focus on the White House state visit itself, Xi’s first since 2015.
Trump, who has referred to the U.S. and China as the “G2,” often touts his personal relationship with his “good friend” Xi, and the two leaders appeared warm and friendly at their last meeting in Beijing in May.
“It was quite astounding to see the chemistry between those two. And it’ll be even more astounding when Xi comes to the White House,” said Orville Schell, the director of the Center on U.S.-China Relations at the Asia Society, a global nonprofit based in New York.
As he meets with Xi this week, Trump wants “the ability to declare victory, regardless of the substance,” Carlson said.
That has raised concerns about what Trump might offer Xi in exchange for a perceived win, particularly when it comes to the Beijing-claimed island of Taiwan. Trump has described a pending $14 billion U.S. arms package for Taiwan as a potential “negotiating chip” with Xi, who has ramped up military pressure on the self-ruling island democracy.
Ideally, China would like the U.S. to end Taiwan arms sales and express clear opposition to Taiwan independence. But “we’re realistic,” said Zhao Hai, vice president of the Chinese Institute of Hong Kong, a think tank that serves as a branch of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government research institution.
“So far, the outcome has been quite good for China, which is the pause on U.S. export of military equipment,” he said. “If we can extend that pause and even cancel some of the more offensive weaponry, that would be better.”
Writing Wednesday in the Chinese Communist Party’s official People’s Daily newspaper, China’s ambassador to the U.S., Xie Feng, said Taiwan was one of China’s “red lines” in any discussions with the U.S., along with human rights.
A senior administration official told NBC News that Trump will make a determination about a new Taiwan arms package “in a fairly short time.”
The official also noted that Trump approved $11.1 billion in arms sales to Taiwan in December, the largest arms package Taiwan has received.
Trump approved more arms sales to Taiwan during his first term than any other president in history, the official said.
Trump’s comments on Taiwan have unnerved key U.S. allies in Asia who depend on Washington for security in the face of growing Chinese aggression. In a joint statement Monday, the U.S. reiterated its commitment to the defense of South Korea and Japan, and the three countries expressed support for Taiwan.
Xi has his own domestic problems, especially an economy weighed down by slowing growth, a property crisis and sluggish consumer spending. But on the international stage, Carlson said, he “doesn’t have to do anything to be in a stronger position because the American position keeps on eroding” as Trump alienates long-standing allies.
In the weeks leading up to his U.S. visit, Xi has had his busiest foreign travel schedule since before the pandemic, shoring up ties with countries from Kyrgyzstan to Egypt to India. His flurry of diplomacy comes as he tries to portray China as a more stabilizing global influence than the U.S., whose war against Iran has caused an international energy crisis.
The Iran war, now in its seventh month, has significantly depleted U.S. munitions — underscoring Washington’s dependence on Beijing, which has a near-monopoly on the rare-earth and critical minerals that are crucial for replenishing U.S. weapons stockpiles and is using it as leverage.
“The United States doesn’t hold all the cards — in fact, maybe not even the preponderance of the cards,” Schell told NBC News last month.
Schell, who was in Beijing for the May summit, said Trump, who campaigned on aggressive levies against China, has gone “from bullying mode into pander mode.” That reflects the “power shift” that has occurred between Beijing and Washington since Trump’s first term in office, he said.
“China has chokeholds now,” Schell said, citing rare earth minerals, electric vehicle technology and other strategic areas that Beijing dominates. “And I think Trump recognized that.”
White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly told NBC News that the Iran war had not significantly depleted U.S. munitions.
“The United States Military has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief’s strategic goals and beyond,” she wrote in an email message.
Trump’s openness to diplomacy with Beijing is increasingly reflected in American public opinion. According to poll results released Monday by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, more than half of Americans support cooperation and engagement with China, including 4 in 10 Republicans.
There remains strong unease, however, around Chinese investment in the U.S., particularly Trump’s suggestion that he would not oppose Chinese automakers’ building cars in the country. On Monday, more than two dozen Democratic lawmakers urged Trump to maintain an effective ban on Chinese automakers in the U.S. market, which their American rivals are pushing to make official.
It’s unclear whether Xi will be accompanied by business leaders as Trump was when he went to Beijing. On the U.S. side, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Apple’s Tim Cook, both of whom were in Beijing, are among the executives expected to attend a state dinner for Xi on Thursday.

articles.title_zh: Ukraine sent two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea, Zelenskiy says
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine sent two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea, Zelenskiy says
By Tom Balmforth and Brenda Goh
UNITED NATIONS/SEOUL, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Ukraine has transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Wednesday in an address to the United Nations General Assembly.
"Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea," said Zelenskiy in his speech.
"These guys are not easy to capture alive. One of them, when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him die."
Zelenskiy did not provide more details about the return. Ukraine captured the two North Koreans in Russia's Kursk region in January last year. They were the first North Korean soldiers to be apprehended alive since the country joined the Russia-Ukraine war in 2024.
Zelenskiy said at the time that he would hand them over to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un if he could facilitate their exchange for Ukrainians held captive in Russia.
Human rights groups, however, urged him to repatriate them to South Korea citing the risks of punishments the soldiers faced. South Korean media reported that the two captured soldiers had expressed their desire to defect to South Korea.
South Korea's foreign ministry said it would not be able to confirm the matter, including details such as the timing of their return, citing the safety of the soldiers and their families. The country's unification ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
South Korea in June said it would accept all North Korean prisoners of war who fought for Russia and opposed any repatriation of them to Russia or North Korea.
Zelenskiy also criticised North Korea for sending its troops to fight for Russia.
"This is madness too. Why should Koreans give their lives in a war against Ukraine? Kim Jong Un uses them like currency. And he gets something in return," he said.
North Korea has sent around 14,000 to 15,000 soldiers since 2024 to support Russia's war against Ukraine, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates. Most of them have been deployed in the Russian region of Kursk, where they helped Moscow's forces repel a Ukrainian incursion.
The country has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery and mortar rounds, ballistic missiles, long-range artillery and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments.
(Reporting by Brenda Goh and Joyce Lee in Seoul and Tom Balmforth in New York; Editing by Stephen Coates)

articles.title_orig: Pentagon investigates after China obtains parts from F-35 stealth fighter jet
articles.title_zh: Pentagon investigates after China obtains parts from F-35 stealth fighter jet
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON – The Pentagon is investigating how parts of the nation's most advanced fighter jet ended up in Hong Kong, with a news outlet reporting Wednesday that China has obtained the F-35 equipment.
The F-35 Joint Program Office said in a statement that it and the Defense Department are aware of “a shipment issue" with F-35 components.
“We are actively working with U.S. authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the office said.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles acknowledged that the jet components ended up in Hong Kong when responding to questions from reporters Tuesday. But he denied that the missing parts were “sensitive equipment.”
Australia is one of several nations whose militaries operate the stealth fighter jet.
“Yeah, so we are obviously working with the United States and obviously with its prime contractor Lockheed Martin, in respect of this,” Marles said.
He added: “My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here or sensitive parts. Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Lockheed did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Wednesday, when Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in Washington for a state visit with President Donald Trump. The Associated Press sent requests for comment to the Chinese embassy and Hong Kong's trade office in Washington.
Bloomberg reported Wednesday that China has the F-35 parts — a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door — after the shipment was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong while on the way from Australia to the United States for either repair or disposal months ago. It was not clear how the shipment was diverted.
Politico earlier reported that it prompted a congressional inquiry over concerns that China could have access to key components of the highly classified technology.
Beijing has kept tight control over Hong Kong since the territory was returned from British rule in 1997. Hong Kong cannot maintain its own military or conduct its own diplomacy.
The first F-35 Lightning strike fighter rolled off an assembly line in Texas about 20 years ago and was hailed as a technological leap. Since then, more than 1,200 of the stealth jets have been made and 19 countries have placed orders for the planes, according to the Congressional Research Service.
China already may have had at least some intelligence, albeit several years old, on the planes already. The Defense Science Board, which advises the Pentagon, released a report in 2013 alleging that Chinese cyberattacks accessed data from dozens of Pentagon programs, including the joint strike fighter.
The F-35 is “widely recognized as America’s best and most advanced fighter jet,” according to Bradley Bowman, senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington-based think tank.
Bowman told the AP in November that American military systems are constantly being updated and improved, counteracting any possible secrets stolen years ago.
Described as a fifth-generation fighter, the F-35's technologies include stealth coatings as well as advanced radar and sensors, according to the Congressional Research Service.
Bowman said the plane has advanced sensors to better detect enemies as well as networking capabilities to communicate with allied planes and ground forces during combat.
Associated Press writer Didi Tang contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: 8 Sailors in U.S.S. Lincoln Strike Group Attempted Suicide, Navy Says
articles.title_zh: 8 Sailors in U.S.S. Lincoln Strike Group Attempted Suicide, Navy Says
articles.content_orig:
Eight US navy personnel assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group have attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran, Hung Cao, the acting US navy secretary, revealed in a letter to the US senator Kirsten Gillibrand on Tuesday.
“Since the beginning of Lincoln’s deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group,” Cao wrote, responding on behalf of US defense secretary Pete Hegseth to Gillibrand’s inquiry about the quality of life aboard the fleet. “This number includes the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons.”
CNN first reported on Cao’s response to Gillibrand.
The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days, disembarked on 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid the unresolved war.
In August, two military newspapers reported on sailors’ deteriorating mental health, including multiple attempts to jump overboard. The reports prompted outcry from Democrats, who called for an investigation of the conditions onboard.
In March, one sailor’s attempt to go overboard was thwarted by shipmates, according to Cao. In August, one sailor did go overboard. The individual was rescued and received medical treatment, before being “transferred off-ship for follow-up care”, Cao wrote.
MS Now also reported in August on alarming allegations of mold in the ship’s showers and dwindling supplies of food and soap, among other basic necessities.
The number of entrée options was temporarily reduced from two to one, Cao wrote in his letter, a measure “implemented to optimize endurance and ensure sustained time on station”. He said four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.
He acknowledged certain delays in replenishing crew supplies.
As details of low morale trickled out of the Lincoln, Hegseth downplayed the media coverage, saying news outlets “completely misrepresented” the situation. “We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” he told reporters in August.
“What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as ‘fake news’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members,” Gillibrand said in a Wednesday statement to the Guardian. “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect. That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.”
“The Navy and the Navy secretary are very committed to sailor health, wellbeing and morale,” a US navy official told the Guardian on Wednesday.

China already may have had at least some intelligence, albeit several years old, on the planes already. The Defense Science Board, which advises the Pentagon, released a report in 2013 alleging that Chinese cyberattacks accessed data from dozens of Pentagon programs, including the joint strike fighter.
The F-35 is “widely recognized as America’s best and most advanced fighter jet,” according to Bradley Bowman, senior director of the Center on Military and Political Power at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington-based think tank.
Bowman told the AP in November that American military systems are constantly being updated and improved, counteracting any possible secrets stolen years ago.
Described as a fifth-generation fighter, the F-35’s technologies include stealth coatings as well as advanced radar and sensors, according to the Congressional Research Service.
Bowman said the plane has advanced sensors to better detect enemies as well as networking capabilities to communicate with allied planes and ground forces during combat.

articles.title_zh: Pentagon investigates after China obtains parts from F-35 stealth fighter jet
articles.content_orig:
The Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, has said.
Marles said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” would be reviewed, but claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend.
The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.
The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.
“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.
“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained one of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.
The US Department of War and F-35 Joint Program Office confirmed they were aware of the “shipment issue”.
“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the spokesperson said.
While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.
Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.
“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.
Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence organisations that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.
Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.
More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.
Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.
Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.
“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the aircraft,” he said.
“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F-35 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”

articles.content_orig: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington Wednesday evening for his first state visit in more than a decade. At the same time, a federal judge heard arguments in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico challenging President Trump banning the outlets from the White House. Liz Landers reports. Geoff Bennett: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington this evening for his first state visit in more than a decade. And at the same time, a federal judge today heard arguments in a lawsuit brought by CNN, MS NOW and Politico challenging President Trump banning them from the White House. Our Liz Landers is at the White House covering both stories, and she joins us now. So, Liz, we will start with this state visit. What is the focus of it? Liz Landers: Yes, Geoff, President Trump is greeting leader Xi right now at Joint Base Andrews here in Washington for an arrival ceremony that has all the pomp and circumstance of this major state visit. This is the first time that Xi has been to the White House since 2015. And President Trump visited China back in May and was not awarded this same kind of pomp, circumstance and arrival. In particular, Xi did not greet him when he landed there in China back in May. You're seeing some of those images now. I will remind our viewers that those images are from several months ago because the White House TV pool is still not covering the president's events today. We believe that there are going to be a number of issues that will be addressed during this visit. A senior administration official told us earlier that AI, artificial intelligence, of course, will be on the top of the list, also some of these export controls that the United States has on our computing chips and selling those to China. The possibility of reducing tariffs on some goods is apparently going to come up, and also political prisoners. Several China watchers and experts that I have spoken with don't really think that this meeting is going to be so much about deliverables as it is about continuing to forge that personal relationship that President Trump has with leader Xi. I spoke earlier today with Kyle Chan. He's a fellow at the Brookings institute. And he was actually talking about these export controls, saying that matters less and less for the Chinese government because they are going all out to build their own AI chips themselves. And when it comes to artificial intelligence in particular, you heard some of that addressed from the U.N. today in Nick's story. China is not interested in a joint slowdown of AI development, according to Chan. He says that they're more worried about cyber risks, hacking companies, and they don't share, China does not share the same concerns that we have heard from U.S. AI companies and leaders recently that robots, AI may kill us all in the near future. Geoff, one more thing I want to add. Not everybody is happy about this visit and all of the accoutrements that are being laid out for President Xi. Republican Senator Wicker, he's the chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, says that he would have advised against this lavish welcome to what he calls a brutal dictator. Geoff Bennett: And, Liz, there's a state dinner tomorrow evening. Who is expected to be in attendance? Liz Landers: Well, Geoff, as you would imagine, with all of this talk of AI and technology, there are leaders from several major business companies and AI companies that are going to be at the White House tomorrow. A senior administration official says that Jeff Bezos will be there, as well as Elon Musk, Michael Dell, Jensen Huang of Nvidia, a chipmaker, and Sam Altman of OpenAI. The first lady, Melania Trump, said in a FOX News interview today that President Trump wanted to have the state dinner because they have a great relationship. She said that she's been involved in every detail of the planning for the state dinner tomorrow night. And she also -- and I'd also just add that this is only the second state dinner that President Trump has now had in his second term in office, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: All right, Liz, in the minute we have left, bring us up to speed on this lawsuit involving the three news organizations that were banned from the White House by President Trump. Liz Landers: There was a hearing on this, this afternoon, and the judge in this case, a district judge here in Washington, said right off the bat that he was skeptical of the argument that the Trump administration, that the Trump White House is making here on due process grounds. It sounds like the judge believes that the due process of these news organizations was violated. The government is arguing in a filing that they issued late last night that news organizations failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House. This has now turned into a conversation about national security. That is what the president and the administration are arguing is at stake here, that these news organizations somehow violated national security there. The judge also seemed skeptical of that, Geoff. We still do not have an answer from the judge as to whether the ban on Politico, CNN, and MS NOW will be lifted. Geoff Bennett: Liz Landers outside the West Wing at the White House for us tonight. Liz, thanks so much. Liz Landers: Of course.

articles.title_zh: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in United States for state visit
articles.content_orig:
Sept. 23 (UPI) -- U.S. President Donald Trump greeted President Xi Jinping of China on Wednesday evening as the Chinese leader arrived at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, marking the start of a three-day state visit.
The tarmac greeting was a rare gesture for an incumbent U.S. president to a foreign leader. Trump and first lady Melania Trump met Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on a red carpet as the U.S. Air Force band performed the countries' national anthems. The ceremony also included a cannon salute, a 21-person honor cordon, color guards and a flyover by two B1 bombers.
There will be another ceremony Thursday morning at the White House featuring more than 500 U.S. service members. The presidents will meet Thursday afternoon with a state dinner Thursday night.
Both Republicans and Democrats have criticized the visit and the lavishness of Trump's treatment of the Chinese leader, The Hill reported . Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said onthe Senate floor Tuesday that Trump should remember that Xi "is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America."
A statement by a group of Senate Democrats including Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Chris Coons, D-Del., also criticized Trump's red-carpet treatment of the Chinese leader.
"President Xi gets the royal treatment while President Trump hurls threats and wages trade wars on allies like Canada," they wrote. "This is not leadership, and Americans deserve better."
The Democrats called on Trump to end China's access "to the advanced chips and manufacturing equipment it needs to build dangerous AI systems," stand with Taiwan against China and press Xi to stop supporting Russia's war in Ukraine.
The trip marks XI's first state visit to the United States in 11 years.

articles.title_orig: Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
articles.title_zh: Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
articles.content_orig:
Meta announced a slate of new wearables during its annual Meta Connect showcase on Wednesday. The star of the event was the new Meta VR Glasses, which pack virtual reality tech into a lightweight smart glasses-style frame with a tethered puck. Meta also announced new pairs of screen-free smart glasses, along with some new AI features and style and frame options.
Meta Connect 2026: The 7 biggest announcements
This year’s Meta Connect featured a new lightweight VR wearable and camera-free Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses.
You can catch up on all the highlights from this year’s Meta Connect below.
Meta’s latest wearable offers full virtual reality in a smart glasses-style form factor. Unlike a typical VR headset, the VR Glasses don’t have any straps, and Meta says they’re “five times lighter than Meta Quest 3” at just 100g. Similar to Google’s Project Aura, the glasses are tethered to a pocket-sized puck with the compute hardware, battery, and storage, including a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite, 128GB of storage, and 12GB of RAM. The 5K micro OLED “Infinite Display” has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye, with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.
The Meta VR Glasses are launching in spring 2027 for $1,299, pricier than the Meta Ray-Ban Display but less expensive than the Apple Vision Pro, while offering similar features. Users can connect the glasses to a Mac or Windows laptop for use as a virtual external display, with an option for a virtual surface keyboard and touchpad.
The VR Glasses also have access to the full Meta Quest catalog of apps and games and support for Xbox Cloud Gaming. Meta says the glasses are “the first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device ever,” and users will be able to watch “immersive live sports” with them as well as 3D movies. They even have a “hologram” feature that creates a “photorealistic digital version of your face” for using in calls while wearing the glasses, reminiscent of the “personas” on the Apple Vision Pro.
Meta is launching camera-free smart glasses
The highlight of the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is the feature they don’t have: built-in cameras. You can use them for things like listening to music, taking calls, or chatting with an AI assistant, but they can’t take pictures or record video — features that have sparked privacy and harassment concerns around Meta’s other glasses.
Meta says the new audio-only glasses are also its “lightest, slimmest AI glasses yet,” weighing just 43g. They offer up to 12 hours of battery life per charge, or 48 hours with the charging case. The Ray-Ban Meta Audio will launch on October 13th starting at $349 with 23 different color and lens combinations.
Refreshed Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 arrive with battery and design upgrades
Meta launched an updated version of its main Ray-Ban Meta glasses, starting at $449. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 offer up to nine hours of battery life, one hour more than the Gen 2. They also have “a new customizable action button for instant access to Meta AI” and a new six-mic array that Meta says “cuts more than 90% of background noise.”
The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 has a slimmer design than the Gen 2 as well, with 27 color and lens combinations, including new Zena and Aviator frame styles. Notably, one thing that hasn’t changed is the built-in LED light that indicates when the glasses are recording, which Meta rolled out a privacy fix for last month.
Budget glasses launch along with new glasses styles
Alongside its pricier Ray-Ban glasses, Meta also announced some updates to its in-house line of glasses. It’s launching a new lower-cost version of the Meta Adventurer, which will start at $249 for a basic design with black frames and gray lenses, launching October 23rd.
Meta is also introducing a new “Mix & Match” program for customizing its glasses with different frames, lenses, and case colors. Plus, its EssilorLuxottica collection is getting two new styles, Capri and Nova, and the Kylie Jenner Starfire frames are getting a new ivory colorway. Meta’s also launching a new collaboration collection with Lisa of Blackpink.
Meta Glasses are expanding to more countries starting today, too, including Singapore, South Korea, Mexico, and the United Arab Emirates, with availability in Brazil “coming soon.”
Meta Ray-Ban Display is coming to more regions with some new features
A year after they originally launched, the Meta Ray-Ban Display are coming to more regions. The glasses are on sale in the UK and Canada starting today, and they’ll be available in France, Italy, and Germany starting on October 13th. Meta’s also introducing online ordering for customers in those regions and the US.
Meta’s launching a new Explore app for Display glasses where users will be able to “browse and use a growing selection of experiences built for your glasses.” The Meta Ray-Ban Display is also getting photo editing, an improved calendar, and mirrored phone notifications. Plus, Meta says the “hologram” feature launching on its VR Glasses is rolling out on the Meta Ray-Ban Display “in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”
After launching its new Muse assistant earlier this month, Meta says it’s “working on” bringing the AI to its smart glasses. When it arrives on the glasses, Muse will be able to do things like guide your workouts, log meals, book appointments, and “help buy products you see.”
Meta also announced some new features for Muse, including video calls with a customizable live avatar of the AI. Plus, Muse agents are getting their own email addresses for completing tasks and communicating with users.
Meta is making an AI ‘charm’
Mark Zuckerberg teased one last device, Muse Charm, a small AI gadget that houses the Muse agent and looks a little bit like a supersized Tamagotchi. More details will be shared “soon,” he said, but the product is supposed to ship in time for the holiday season.

articles.title_zh: Meta VR Glasses Officially Announced, Shipping Spring 2027 For $1300
articles.content_orig:
Meta VR Glasses were just officially announced. Priced at $1300, they have 2.4K micro-OLED displays, weigh 100 grams, and are powered by a tethered puck with Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset.
The puck runs the same operating system as Quest 3, and supports all the same content, rendered at notably higher resolution thanks to a combination of the more powerful chipset (essentially an XR2 Gen 3 by a different name) and eye-tracked foveated rendering. It features 12GB of RAM and 128GB of storage, and there's a microSD slot in the puck to expand it.
The caveat to the content compatibility is that Meta VR Glasses do not come with controllers by default, but you can buy Touch Plus controllers separately (available in a new all-black color), or pair the controllers from your existing Quest 3 or Quest 3S, and there'll be a bundle with controllers "in some retail channels".
The stark difference between Meta VR Glasses and any Quest, however, is the split architecture, and the dramatic reduction in weight and bulk this enables.
Meta VR Glasses have no onboard computing, not even a tracking coprocessor, and thus entirely rely on the puck, which provides both power and data over a thin and flexible fiber optic cable.
The visor has an open-periphery design, so you naturally see the real world to your sides and below you. It's built with a magnesium alloy that minimizes weight while also enabling a fanless, passively cooled design that weighs "around" 100 grams.
Another key difference is the display and field of view. With dual 120Hz 2412×2288 HDR micro-OLED displays, Meta VR Glasses have the highest resolution of any Meta headset to date, and are the company's first non-LCD headset since the original Oculus Quest.
The displays support the Dolby Vision HDR format, Meta says it's the first VR device to be IMAX Enhanced certified.
The form factor brings a major optical compromise, though: the field of view. Meta advertises 70° horizontal × 66° vertical (equating to 87° diagonal) compared to the roughly 110° horizontal × 96° vertical of Quest 3.
The lower field of view will make Meta VR Glasses feel far less immersive than a Quest headset when the optional light blockers are attached for fully immersive experiences. But, somewhat ironically given the name of the product, Meta VR Glasses should shine without the light blockers in passthrough mixed reality, where a natural view of your periphery is arguably preferable to darkness.
Meta plans to market the product as "a private cinema, multiple virtual monitor workspace, and game console in one device that fits in your bag".
Essentially, Meta VR Glasses at its core is the same product proposition as the Xreal Aura Android XR glasses but with a VR-style passthrough display system that offers a larger field of view (87° diagonal vs Xreal's 70°), higher resolution, and full opacity, alongside the inclusion of eye tracking and optional tracked controllers. We do not yet know the price of Xreal Aura.
To expand the library of content available to all Meta VR Glasses buyers, Meta announced a swathe of new hand tracking VR and mixed reality games, including a new hand-tracked Beat Saber mode called Flux. You can read about the gaming announcements here.
For the first time for a Meta standalone device, you can also plug in any USB-C DisplayPort device to the puck and have it shown as a huge virtual screen in Meta VR Glasses, without the need for a capture card.
Meta VR Glasses will also feature the first implementation of Hologram, the company's productization of its Codec Avatars research. Similar to Apple Vision Pro's Personas, it will let you join flatscreen WhatsApp video calls as a photorealistic face-tracked avatar, and appear as a realistic full-scale avatar for other Meta VR Glasses (and eventually Quest 3) owners.
However, at launch in spring, your spatial Hologram will be a "2.5D" stereoscopic video stream, at true scale but only seen as a front-angle view. Even if you change your perspective, the Hologram will stay as a head-on perspective. Meta says it plans to evolve Hologram over time to become a truly 6DoF 3D system, at which point it will become the default platform-level avatar experience for its VR platform, effectively superseding the cartoon Meta Avatars.

articles.title_orig: Meta Announces ‘VR Glasses’ Next-Gen XR Headset, Priced at $1,300
articles.title_zh: Meta Announces ‘VR Glasses’ Next-Gen XR Headset, Priced at $1,300
articles.content_orig:
Meta today unveiled its long-awaited next-gen mixed reality headset: Meta VR Glasses.
Previously known under the codename ‘Project Phoenix’, Meta VR Glasses was announced today, but isn’t launching just yet; the compute puck-tethered device is slated to go one sale sometime in Spring 2027, priced at $1,300.
While we’re still waiting on a precise release date, Meta did reveal an avalanche of details on the hardware alongside a slate of new immersive and casual viewing content coming to the headset. You can catch Road to VR’s hands-on with Meta VR Glasses here.
Meta VR Glasses – Hardware
Meta VR Glasses feature what the company is calling its ‘5K Infinite Display’, which uses micro-OLED panels, offering a 5.5MP (2,412 x 2,288) per-eye resolution at 37 pixels per degree (PPD)—notably higher than Quest 3’s 25 PPD.
In fact, despite being significant lower resolution than Vison Pro’s 11.7MP per-eye resolution, Meta says VR Glasses has a higher PPD (34 vs 37) because VR Glasses spreads its pixels over a tighter field-of-view of about 88° diagonally (H70° × V66°).
That’s not the only thing that’s smaller. Meta VR Glasses weigh about 100g on the head, as the battery and compute have been moved to a separate puck connected to a proprietary port via an optical cable.
Inside that pocketable puck (~300g) is Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Reality Elite processor (XR2 Gen 3) and a battery with a claimed 3+ hours of mixed use. The puck can also be used charged while in use, when plugged into its included 45W USB-C power supply.
Lenses can be manually adjusted for a interpupillary distance (IPD) range between 56–70mm, and can also be fit with prescription inserts from Meta partner Zenni Optical.
As for sensors, VR Glasses comes with a wide array: eye-tracking cameras for UI selection and biometric unlock, front and downward-facing camera sensors for a wider hand-tracking range, and full color passthrough sensors offering 26 PPD. It of course also does the same capable 6DOF spatial tracking pioneered in the company’s Quest lineup.
Like its Meta Ray-Ban Display smart glasses, Meta VR Glasses support a mix of gaze and hand gestures: look to highlight a button, pinch your fingers together to select, rub your thumb up or down, or side to side to scroll through content.
While that mix of eye and hand-tracking is its main input scheme (i.e., not shipping with physical controllers), Meta VR Glasses do support Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, which the company says you can either buy separately or actually use from your existing Meta Quest 3 or 3S.
Meta is also baking in Surface Keyboard—released earlier this year on Quest—to turn any flat surface into a keyboard and trackpad, which comes in addition to being able to pair Bluetooth peripherals like keyboards, gamepads, and more.
Meta VR Glasses are being offered in two sizes (for different head sizes), Standard and Large, which are notably two separate SKUs. Only one storage option has been announced thus far: 128GB internal storage with the option to expand up to 1TB via the puck’s microSD card slot.
When they do launch next spring, Meta VR Glasses are targeting broad international availability, with supported regions including: US, UK, Canada, Mexico, Germany, Poland, France, Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, Switzerland, Austria, Ireland, Iceland, Finland, Spain, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand.
Meta VR Glasses – Software & Games
Meta VR Glasses run the same OS and store as Quest, so the entire Quest catalog of VR games and apps are there.
At least in terms of gaming without Touch controllers, Meta has promised 75+ games and apps optimized for hand gesture input, with its headliners including a modified version of Beat Saber for hand-tracking, 3D puzzle game Dragon Grove, courtroom sim Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney, Dual Destinies, and a modified version of Tetris Effect for hand-tracking.
Meta says all of your usual streaming apps will be there at launch: Disney+ and Peacock, both with 3D, plus HBO, YouTube, Prime Video and more. Other streaming services can also be accessed via the built-in browser.
Meta VR Glasses is also technically an ‘IMAX Enhanced’ certified VR device supporting Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos immersive spatial audio, which means you’ll be able to watch select films in IMAX’s exclusive expanded aspect ratio.
Outside of casual gaming, video, and 180-degree immersive sports content, which you also find on Quest, Meta is leaning particularly hard into productivity.
The device supports wireless multi-screen virtual desktop streaming from Mac, PC or phone, opening it up to be more of a general computing device. Native DisplayPort-In also allows you to directly wire into laptops, consoles and handhelds.

articles.title_orig: US, China agree to extend trade truce by two months, work on bigger deal, Bessent says
articles.title_zh: US, China agree to extend trade truce by two months, work on bigger deal, Bessent says
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. and China have extended a truce to keep tariffs lower for longer and rare earths flowing, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday local time.
He was speaking on Fox News, as Chinese President Xi Jinping landed in Washington, D.C. for a state visit through Friday.
Xi and Trump agreed to a one-year trade truce at a meeting in South Korea last October. The deal, which was set to expire in November, will now be extended to Jan. 10, Bessent said. He added that Beijing needs to fulfill more deliverables.
Ahead of this week's summit, many had expected the truce would be extended by six months or longer.
Chinese state media did not immediately note Bessent's comments on the trade truce.
Xi said in an official readout for his arrival that he is confident the visit will produce "fruitful results" for both sides. He said the two countries should be partners, not rivals, and work to build a stable relationship where competition and differences are managed. The readout did not mention tariffs, rare earths or artificial intelligence.
Footage streamed on China's state broadcaster showed U.S. President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump meeting Xi and First Lady of China Peng Liyuan at the foot of the Chinese leader's jet. The video did not show the U.S. and Chinese leaders shaking hands — it focused on Xi and his wife shaking hands with two children presenting them each with bouquets.
After greeting Xi, Trump told reporters he would discuss the Iran war with the Chinese leader, among "many other subjects."
Bessent met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York ahead of Xi's arrival in the U.S. The two sides discussed setting up an alert system for AI incidents, according to Bessent.
While executives of major U.S. tech companies plan to join a summit dinner on Thursday, none of their Chinese counterparts are expected to attend.
Politburo Standing Committee Member Cai Qi and China's top diplomat Wang Yi accompanied Xi, according to state media.
—CNBC's Ashlee Trujillo contributed to this report.
